info.name: AI Operations Copilot
info.description:
AI-powered backend service that helps an operations team answer customer and operational queries.

## Setup

1. Start the service: `npm install && npm start`
2. The `baseUrl` variable defaults to `http://localhost:3000` — change it in the collection variables if you run on a different port.

No authentication is required.

## Where to start

Open **Copilot → The three example questions** and run them in order. Those are the queries from the problem statement and they exercise the whole system: tool routing, deterministic diagnostics, and grounded answers.

## How to read a response

`POST /api/query` returns an envelope:

- `answer` — the prose answer, the thing a human reads.
- `meta` — provider, tool rounds, stop reason, latency, token usage.
- `trace` — the audit trail: every tool call, its arguments, its latency, and which diagnostic rules fired.

Add `?format=text` to any query request to get just the answer as plain text.

## A note on the design

The LLM routes and phrases; it does not diagnose. Whether an order is in trouble is decided by deterministic rules over the actual records, which is why `trace[].finding_codes` is the field to check when you want to know *why* an answer says what it says.

## Seeded orders worth trying

| Order | What it demonstrates |
|---|---|
| `4521` | Delivered cleanly — healthy, no findings. |
| `1289` | Paid, warehouse hold, no delivery scheduled. |
| `2231` | Paid and dispatched, delivery overdue. |
| `9999` | Does not exist — graceful failure. |

request.description:
**The question that shapes the architecture.**

This is not retrieval — it is a diagnosis. Answering it requires noticing that two subsystems disagree: payment says captured, fulfilment says nothing scheduled.

That judgement is made by deterministic rules, not by the model. Check `trace[].finding_codes`: you will see `PAID_NO_DELIVERY_SCHEDULED` and `WAREHOUSE_HOLD`. The model's only job was to phrase them.

The practical consequence: the amount, the date and the cause in the answer are facts read from rows. They cannot be hallucinated, because the model never had the freedom to invent them.

query.description: `text` for the bare answer, `json` for the full envelope. Overrides the Accept header.

request.description:
Returns only the answer, as `text/plain`.

The text is byte-identical to the JSON `answer` field — the format changes the envelope, never the answer. The trace is still computed and logged server-side; it is simply omitted from the response.

Error responses honour the format too, so a text client gets a plain sentence rather than JSON on a 400 or 502.

response.name: 200 — plain text
response.body:
The payment status for order #4521 (ORD-4521) is PAID.

Payment summary:
- Status: PAID (State: CAPTURED)
- Amount paid: INR 1,20,946
- Method: CREDIT_CARD
- Payment attempts: 1 successful attempt (0 failures)

The payment is fully captured and the order is marked healthy with no outstanding issues.

request.description:
Standard HTTP content negotiation. `Accept: text/plain` gets the bare answer.

JSON remains the default: a bare `Accept: */*` — what browsers and `fetch` send — does not trigger text mode. Only an explicit `text/plain` preference does.

request.description:
Order 9999 does not exist.

The tool returns a structured error, which goes back to the model **as data** rather than being thrown. The model then reports the absence honestly.

This returns HTTP 200: the request was valid and the system answered it correctly. The failure is in the data, not the call — and it is visible in `trace[].error_code`.

item.name: Orders (no LLM)
item.description:
The same tools the model calls, reached directly. No model in the path, so these return in about a millisecond and cost nothing.

An ops dashboard rendering an order page should use these. They are also the fastest way to debug a suspicious answer: if the REST endpoint shows the same thing, the problem is in the data or the rules, not the model.

`:id` accepts `4521`, `#4521` or `ORD-4521`.

request.description:
The primary tool, called directly. Returns order, customer, payment, delivery, open tickets, a `health` verdict and the `findings` array.

`findings` is the interesting part — it is produced by deterministic rules, sorted most severe first, and each entry carries `evidence` (the exact fields the rule fired on) and `recommended_action` (what to do about it).

Defaults to order `1289`. Try `4521` for a healthy order that returns an empty `findings` array.

request.description:
The control case. Order 4521 was delivered cleanly, so `findings` is empty and `health` is `HEALTHY`.

Worth checking: a copilot that manufactures concerns about healthy orders is as useless as one that misses real problems.

Every payment attempt for an order, oldest first — including failures, retries, gateway transaction ids, failure codes and refunded amounts.

The `summary` block collapses the history into a current verdict: an order whose first attempt failed and whose retry succeeded reports as `CAPTURED`, not `FAILED`.

Courier, AWB, promised date, attempt history, current location, and a computed `is_overdue` / `days_overdue`.

Try order `1289` instead: it returns `delivery_record: null` with a `note` explaining that nothing is scheduled. That explicit null is what lets the copilot say "there is no delivery record" rather than guessing.

request.description:
Order 1289 has no delivery record. The endpoint returns 200 with `delivery_record: null` and a `note` — absence is data, not an error.

This matters: a 404 here would be ambiguous between "no such order" and "no delivery yet", and the copilot needs to tell those apart.

Chronological event log: placed, paid, dispatched, delayed, refunded, and so on — each with a timestamp, type, description and source (`system`, `courier`, `warehouse`, `ops`, `customer`).

Related tickets are included alongside.

request.description:
**Run this first.** Confirms the service is up and tells you which LLM provider is active.

If `using_mock_fallback` is `true`, no `GEMINI_API_KEY` is configured and the service is serving deterministic templated answers. Everything still works — the answers are just stilted rather than model-written.

The seven read-only functions the model is allowed to call, with the descriptions it routes on.

The model cannot see the dataset — only what these tools return. All seven are read-only, so a hallucinated call is at worst a wasted round trip, never a wrong write.

Shows how a user-typed order reference is canonicalised.

`4521`, `#4521`, `ord-4521` and `Order ORD-4521` all resolve to `ORD-4521`. The `#` is URL-encoded as `%23` here, since a literal `#` would start a URL fragment.
Unknown routes return a structured `NOT_FOUND` error rather than an HTML error page.
